title: Bulking Diet for NZ Gym‑Goers – Clean Bulk Guide
meta_desc: Learn how NZ gym‑goers can bulk cleanly with realistic calorie targets, local high‑protein foods, meal timing tips and affordable supplements.
intro: Building muscle without adding excess fat is possible with a disciplined clean‑bulk approach. This guide breaks down the numbers, the foods you can buy locally and practical steps you can start this week.

sections.heading: Clean Bulk vs Dirty Bulk
sections.body:
A clean bulk focuses on a modest calorie surplus (5‑10 % above maintenance) and nutrient‑dense foods, aiming for muscle gain while keeping fat gain low. A dirty bulk throws calorie counting out the window, relying on any high‑calorie foods – often processed and sugary – which can lead to rapid fat accumulation and later a cutting phase. While a dirty bulk may speed up weight gain, it usually requires a longer cut to shed the extra fat, which can be demotivating and affect hormone balance.

For most NZers balancing work, study or family, a clean bulk is more sustainable. It keeps energy levels steady, supports recovery, and aligns with the typical NZ diet that already includes plenty of fresh produce and lean proteins.
list: Clean bulk: +5‑10 % calories, whole‑food focus, slower but leaner gains.
Dirty bulk: +20‑30 % calories, processed foods, faster weight gain but higher fat.

sections.heading: Setting Your Calorie Surplus
sections.body:
First, estimate your maintenance calories using a simple multiplier (body weight kg × 30‑33 kcal for most active men, 28‑31 kcal for women). Add 250‑500 kcal for a clean bulk. Keep protein at 2.2 g per kg bodyweight, carbs at 4‑5 g per kg, and the remainder from healthy fats.

Tracking your intake for a week with a free app (MyFitnessPal, Cronometer) will reveal if you’re hitting the target. Adjust by 100 kcal each week based on weight changes – aim for 0.25‑0.5 kg gain per week.

sections.heading: Protein Timing and Meal Planning
sections.body:
Research shows that spreading protein intake evenly across 4‑5 meals maximises muscle protein synthesis. Aim for 20‑30 g of high‑quality protein within 2 hours pre‑ and post‑workout. Include a carbohydrate source post‑session to replenish glycogen and support recovery.

A simple weekly plan could look like:
• Breakfast – 40 g oats, 1 cup milk, 2 eggs.
• Mid‑morning snack – Greek yoghurt + banana.
• Lunch – 150 g chicken breast, 200 g sweet potato, veg.
• Pre‑workout (30 min) – 1 slice whole‑grain toast with 30 g Quorn mince.
• Post‑workout – Whey shake (25 g protein) + fruit.
• Dinner – 150 g lean beef, brown rice, broccoli.
• Evening snack – cottage cheese or a small handful of nuts.

Consistent timing helps you hit daily protein goals without feeling overly full.
list: Aim for 0.4‑0.5 g protein per kg bodyweight per meal.
Include carbs around workouts (30‑60 g) for energy and recovery.
Hydrate – at least 3 L water daily, more on heavy training days.

sections.heading: Affordable Supplements & Extra Protein Sources
sections.body:
Supplements can fill gaps but aren’t essential if you hit targets with whole foods. The most cost‑effective options in NZ are:
• Whey protein concentrate – NZ$40 per 1 kg (Bulk Nutrients, The Protein Works). One scoop (~30 g) gives ~24 g protein for about $1.20.
• Milk protein isolate – $45 per 1 kg, useful for night‑time shakes.
• Creatine monohydrate – $20 per 300 g, proven to boost strength and lean mass.

If you prefer plant‑based routes, soy or pea protein powders sit around $35‑$45 per kg. Pair them with a banana or oat milk for a quick post‑workout shake.

Remember, Exercise NZ’s subsidised gym scheme can reduce your membership cost by 40‑70 %, freeing up budget for quality food and supplements.
list: Whey concentrate – $40 /kg, ~24 g protein per scoop.
Creatine monohydrate – $20 /300 g, 5 g daily dose.
